title: Recording restrictions and the Gennett sound
summary: A dance band versus the Wolverines; the drummer and tuba restricted, each trumpet needing its own horn, two sides in a day.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Excuse me - briefly tell the difference between what the Wolverines were doing and what Chubb- Steinberg was doing--- at that time?

Well, we were a straight dance band -- with a little jazz here and there. But, they were a jazz band; that was the difference. But, uh, the difficult part for the recordings in those days, the drummer

couldn't use his base drum because if he hit the base drum too hard, the needle would fly right off the wax. And, any sudden sound like that. So, the drummer had to only use his wood block or his cow bells or his symbols -- he had to play then real softly on the snare drum usually with brushes and the tuba - everybody had tubas in those days -- and the tuba had to be clear across the room because that (demonstration of sound) of a tuba would knock the needle off too. So, they had---
Well, that's why you didn't hear him play it I suppose---

Yeah - well, first they had it all worked out where everybody was supposed to sit and where they stay and, of course, there was no - two horns - now, for instance, we had two trumpets. Two horns--- two trumpets couldn't play in the same horn---

Each one had to have their own. Because if you put two trumpets together in that horn, it made terrible distortion. So, sometimes I would be sitting on a real high stool playing in my horn and the other trumpet player would be down here somewhere -- playing in the horn. So, it was--- it was a tricky thing to do really - the recording. And, uh, the thing that was tricky about it was that you were a nervous wreck about making mistake because once you made a serious mistake,

you blew the whole thing. And, so, it was--- I don't think in any of those days of recording, that we'd ever get more than two numbers. That's one record. We were lucky, if it took us all day -- well, say, five or six, seven hours maybe sometimes to do two sides - that passed--- that they said -- okay. And, you know, they had - if you have listened to those Gennett records, they had a definite sound---
That Gennett Company had a sound that you couldn't miss; it was so far beyond most of the companies at that time.
They were way ahead in jazz records in particular - weren't they?
